chain.label: Up-sloping volcanic terrain along the saddle transition route
chain.trigger: the up-sloping terrain... the accident site was located about 7.5 nautical miles east-northeast from the 13,333-foot peak of the Mauna Loa volcano

chain.label: Operator had no flight plan or procedure for the routinely flown half-island saddle route
chain.trigger: Big Island Air does not have a flight plan covering this half-island tour route... they typically do not notify AFSS of the change

chain.label: Pilot did not obtain the required preflight weather briefing
chain.trigger: the pilot's failure to obtain a preflight weather briefing was a deviation from standard operating procedures

chain.label: Airplane departed about 224 lbs over maximum allowable gross weight
chain.trigger: the airplane's total weight was 7,592 lbs, about 224 lbs over its maximum allowable gross weight

chain.label: VFR tour flight entered instrument meteorological conditions over the volcano's northeast slope
chain.trigger: The Safety Board therefore concludes that on the accident flight, the pilot flew into instrument meteorological conditions (IMC).

caused_by.evidence: On the eastern (windward) side of the island, clouds often form over the up-sloping terrain.
rather than flying from the Hilo area to KOA via the South Point, pilots sometimes fly back to KOA via the saddle route
No evidence exists to indicate that the pilot sought or obtained an updated weather briefing for the accident flight later that afternoon as required by the FAA.

chain.label: Pilot continued the VFR flight into IMC instead of reversing course as company policy required
chain.trigger: it was company policy for pilots to reverse course, as required, to avoid entering IMC... the pilot did not reverse course or take emergency action

caused_by.evidence: witnesses indicated that on the day of the accident, the sky was overcast in the vicinity of the accident site
the FAA has no record of the pilot requesting a weather briefing for either September 25, 1999, flight

chain.label: Pilot did not use available navigational aids and failed to recognize he was nearing high terrain
chain.trigger: If the pilot had been using his navigational aids correctly, he would have realized that he was nearing high terrain and would likely have changed his course.

caused_by.evidence: when he departed visual meteorological conditions and flew into IMC, he should have used the navigational aids to accurately monitor his ground track and altitude
Radar data indicates that at this point in flight, the airplane's track varied little from its predominately west-northwesterly direction.

chain.label: Airplane held a west-northwesterly track off the approved route with ground clearance rapidly decreasing
chain.trigger: During the last few minutes of flight, when the airplane's ground clearance was rapidly decreasing... The accident site was approximately 3.5 miles laterally south of the depicted route segment referred to as segment 'V-T'

caused_by.evidence: the pilot did not reverse course or take emergency action
Both the airplane's altitude and the terrain's elevation were increasing.
The airplane's rate of climb during the last 1/2 minute of flight was consistent with the airplane beginning to operate near its maximum (multiengine) climb performance.

chain.label: Airplane flew into the northeast slope of Mauna Loa at 10,100 feet msl
chain.trigger: About 1726, the accident airplane crashed on the northeast slope of the Mauna Loa volcano at 10,100 feet msl.

caused_by.evidence: the damage signatures were consistent with the impact having occurred while the airplane's wings were within 10 degrees of level at zero pitch

chain.label: Pilot and nine passengers killed; airplane destroyed by impact and postimpact fire
chain.trigger: The pilot and all nine passengers on board were killed, and the airplane was destroyed by impact forces and a postimpact fire.

caused_by.evidence: The airplane was destroyed by impact forces and a severe postimpact fire.
